overview: Genesis Energy is one of New Zealand's four large listed "gentailers," generating and retailing electricity, natural gas and LPG to more than 520,000 customers (FY25) across a single unified Genesis brand (formerly Genesis, Frank and Ecotricity). Its generation portfolio spans the Huntly thermal power station (including three 250 MW Rankine coal/gas units that act as the country's dry-year and winter-peak backstop), three hydro schemes (Tekapo, Tongariro, Waikaremoana), an emerging renewables build (Lauriston solar, Edgecumbe, Foxton, Leeston, Waipipi wind PPA), and a 46% interest in the Kupe oil and gas field. The New Zealand Crown, via the Public Finance Act, is required to hold at least 51% of Genesis's shares, which caps free float and materially shapes governance, capital raising and takeover dynamics.

business_model.summary: Genesis is an integrated generator-retailer ("gentailer"): it generates electricity from a diversified thermal/hydro/renewables portfolio and sells electricity, gas and LPG directly to households and businesses, capturing margin across both the wholesale (generation) and retail (customer) legs of the value chain. Reported EBITDAF was NZ$454m in FY25 (normalised NZ$470m) on revenue of NZ$3.7bn; H1 FY26 (six months to Dec-2025) delivered a record normalised EBITDAF of NZ$307m, up 38% YoY, with gross margin up 27% to NZ$521m and NPAT up 36% to NZ$95m. Wholesale earnings are asset-based and highly weather/hydrology dependent (hydro output ~2.6-3 TWh/yr); retail earnings are recurring but thin-margin and regulated on the lines-charges pass-through side. LPG contributed NZ$65m of gross margin in FY25 and is being split into a standalone business unit from FY26 given declining NZ gas supply.

revenue_streams.name: Retail electricity, gas and LPG (Genesis brand, post Frank/Ecotricity consolidation)
Huntly Firming Options / capacity contracts (HFOs) with Meridian, Mercury, Contact

business_model.customer_type: B2C mass-market residential plus B2B commercial & industrial (C&I) customers; wholesale counterparties are the other major gentailers and large industrials
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% New Zealand — generation assets at Huntly (Waikato), Tekapo/Tongariro/Waikaremoana (hydro), Waipipi (Taranaki wind PPA), Lauriston/Edgecumbe/Foxton/Leeston (solar, Canterbury/Bay of Plenty/Manawatu), and Kupe (Taranaki offshore gas)

main_competitors: Independent retailers (e.g., Electric Kiwi, Flick, Octopus Energy NZ)
NZ Aluminium Smelter / large industrial self-generators
competitive_position.market_position: One of New Zealand's "big four" gentailers; FY25 electricity retail market share 22.9% (down from 24.0% in FY24) and natural gas market share 33.3% (down from 35.6%); ranked first in the energy market for brand equity (43% vs 40% FY24) and for EV plan awareness

moat_factors.description: Huntly's three Rankine units plus Unit 5/6 gas-diesel turbines give Genesis NZ's largest flexible/dispatchable capacity (1,204 MW), able to switch between coal, gas and diesel to firm the grid during dry years and low-wind periods — a role increasingly monetised via 10-year Huntly Firming Options with the other three gentailers, subject to Commerce Commission review
Three hydro schemes spread across the country capture rainfall in different catchments, partially diversifying hydrology risk versus a single-basin operator

Owning both generation and retail lets Genesis internally hedge wholesale price volatility against its own retail book, and the pending non-discrimination regime is designed specifically to blunt this advantage relative to independent retailers

New generation development (consenting, grid connection, capital intensity) is slow and costly, protecting incumbents' installed base even as ~40,000 MW of new projects have been announced across the sector
51% Crown shareholding underpins a BBB+ credit rating and access to capital markets, though it also caps takeover premia and dilutes minority influence over capital allocation

weaknesses: Retail and gas market share both declined in FY25 (electricity 24.0%→22.9%, gas 35.6%→33.3%), suggesting competitive/regulatory pressure
Aging Huntly thermal fleet requires ongoing capex and carries carbon/ETS cost exposure that peers with more renewables-weighted portfolios avoid

Kupe gas field (46% interest) is a depleting asset — KS-9 well underperformance already cut ~$15-20m of FY24 earnings, and Genesis's own reporting assumes Kupe field decommissioning by the early 2030s
Smaller renewables base than Meridian and Mercury historically, requiring an accelerated ~$1.1bn solar build to catch up

growth_drivers: Gen35 strategy Horizon 2 (FY26-FY28): targeting mid-to-upper $500m normalised EBITDAF by FY28 (versus $470m FY25), from average hydro conditions with no major outages

~NZ$2 billion development pipeline spanning Huntly repurposing/firming, grid-scale battery storage (BESS), and renewables, funded in part by the Feb-2026 NZ$400m equity raise ($300m rights offer + $100m placement)

Solar build-out: Lauriston (63 MWp, operating), Edgecumbe (127 MWp, FID due late 2025), Foxton (220 MWp, fast-track consented, construction from 2027), Leeston (67 MWp, plug-and-play acquisition) — targeting up to 500 MW of grid-scale solar by FY28
Huntly Battery Energy Storage System (BESS): Stage 1 (100 MW/200 MWh) due online from Q1 FY27, with a Stage 2 (up to another 200 MWh) under investigation

Huntly Firming Options (HFOs): 10-year capacity agreements signed August 2025 with Meridian, Mercury and Contact (subject to Commerce Commission review) covering 235 MW of Rankine/fuel-reserve capacity through 2035, converting the Rankines from a pure earnings-volatility asset into contracted fee income
Biomass ('Future Fuels') strategy to progressively displace coal at Huntly, with a stated pathway to 300kt pa and term sheets signed with potential biomass suppliers
Electrification of transport (ChargeNet EV charging JV, moved to majority ownership in FY25) and process heat/demand flexibility products (Kinergy/GridSmart hot-water control trial shifted 1.43 GWh)
Castle Hill wind farm (up to 300 MW, consents extended to 2031) and other wind prospects freed up by the Hau Nui divestment, targeting a development pathway to 300 MW of wind

New Zealand's broader 60-95-100 decarbonisation trajectory (60% of energy electric, 95% renewable generation, 100% availability) structurally grows electricity demand that Genesis is positioned to serve

business.description: Hydro output (2.6-3 TWh/yr) and wholesale spot prices are highly weather dependent; FY25 swung from a dry Q1/Q3 to a wet Q2, materially moving quarterly EBITDAF, and winter 2024 saw a genuine supply crunch requiring Genesis to buy incremental Methanex gas to keep Huntly running
Increasing intermittent (solar/wind) generation entering the grid (~80% of ~40,000 MW of announced new projects) is expected to increase price volatility and the amount of firming capacity required

business.risk: Retail and gas market share erosion
business.description: Electricity market share fell to 22.9% (from 24.0%) and gas share to 33.3% (from 35.6%) in FY25 amid competitive and regulatory pressure; brand consolidation (Genesis/Frank/Ecotricity into one brand) cut ~200 retail roles

46%-owned Kupe gas/oil field is in structural decline (KS-9 well failure cost ~$15-20m of FY24 earnings); Genesis's own planning assumes the field's contribution — and NZ baseload gas generation broadly — falls to ~500 GWh pa by the early 2030s

financial.description: Feb-2026 NZ$400m capital raise (1-for-7.9 rights offer at $2.05, 10.8% discount to TERP, plus $100m placement) dilutes non-participating shareholders by up to ~17.4%; used initially to reduce net debt and fund growth capex
~$1.1bn renewables build to FY30 plus Huntly BESS/firming investment and hydro stay-in-business capex (e.g., $95m Waikaremoana upgrade) increase funding needs and near-term free cash flow drag
Board is committed to maintaining a BBB+ credit rating over the long term, which constrains leverage and could cap the pace of growth capex or dividends in a downside scenario

regulatory.risk: Electricity Authority / Commerce Commission gentailer market review
regulatory.description: The joint Energy Competition Task Force (established Aug-2024) is progressing pro-competition interventions intended to be in place by mid-2026, including mandatory non-discrimination obligations preventing gentailers' wholesale arms from favouring their own retail arms over independents, with first compliance reporting due 1 July 2026, and proposals for minimum gentailer trading volumes in the new wholesale hedge product

regulatory.risk: Huntly Firming Options subject to Commerce Commission review
regulatory.description: The 10-year HFO agreements with Meridian, Mercury and Contact — central to monetising Huntly's flexibility role — require Commerce Commission clearance before proceeding

Huntly's coal and gas generation carries direct NZ ETS carbon costs; emissions rise mechanically whenever thermal backup is called on in dry/low-wind periods, creating headline optics risk even as underlying baseload emissions decline

About 60% of 2025 increases in customer electricity bills stem from Commerce Commission-approved lines charges (network costs), a pass-through Genesis does not control but which affects retail competitiveness and customer churn

macro.description: New Zealand's gas supply is down about 40% versus a few years ago; declining gas availability (Kupe and other fields) is driving both higher generation costs (more expensive solid-fuel/coal use) and structural volatility in wholesale gas and electricity prices

As a high-payout utility funding a large capex programme partly via equity and debt, Genesis's cost of capital and dividend attractiveness are sensitive to NZ interest rate moves and investor appetite for yield stocks

Large industrial demand signals (e.g., NZ Aluminium Smelter continuation, Lake Onslow pumped-hydro scheme cancellation) have recently been resolved in Genesis's favour, but electrification-driven demand growth assumptions underpin the capex build-out and could disappoint

macro_factors.industry_outlook: New Zealand electricity demand is expected to grow via electrification of transport and process heat, with the sector needing large amounts of new generation (developers have announced ~40,000 MW of projects, ~80% intermittent solar/wind) and greater firming capacity to maintain the 60-95-100 net zero pathway (60% of energy electric, 95% renewable, 100% reliable) by 2050
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low revenue cyclicality (retail demand is inelastic/essential) but high earnings volatility driven by hydrology, wind and gas supply conditions from quarter to quarter and year to year
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate — high dividend payout ratio makes the stock partly a bond-proxy/yield asset sensitive to NZ interest rates, and the large capex programme relies on debt and equity markets
key_input_costs: Coal (solid-fuel reserve at Huntly, ~500kt-1m tonnes stockpile)
Natural gas (Kupe JV production plus market purchases, e.g., Methanex gas)

recent_developments.event: FY26 full-year results not yet released (Genesis typically reports in late August); the FY26 figures in this analysis are guidance and unaudited quarterly operational data, not audited actuals

Huntly BESS Stage 1 (100 MW / 2hr) commissioning underway; Stage 2 (100 MW / 200 MWh) entered detailed design with a BESS supply contract with Saft commenced; Tihori solar farm (formerly Edgecumbe) on track for COD in Q1 FY28 and Leeston solar FID targeted Q1 FY27

FY26 Q4 performance report: full-year retail electricity netback improved to $175.5/MWh (FY25 $155.3), but total customers fell 5.8% YoY to 490,227 (from 520,519) and total ICPs fell 3.8% to 705,523 - margin quality was prioritised over volume. Rankine output collapsed 70% YoY to 505 GWh with coal firing at 45% of Rankine fuel (FY25 90%), and generation emissions fell 64% to 926 ktCO2

Upgraded FY26 normalised EBITDAF guidance a second time, to NZ$515-545m (from NZ$490-520m set in January 2026, itself up from the original NZ$455-485m), citing cost discipline, improved hydrology and favourable wholesale conditions that reduced thermal generation and lowered fuel and carbon costs

Announced combined NZ$400m equity raise (NZ$300m 1-for-7.9 renounceable rights offer at $2.05/share, 10.8% discount to TERP, plus NZ$100m institutional/broker placement) to reduce net debt and accelerate the Gen35 renewables/firming pipeline; Crown committed to maintain its 51% stake via the Crown Participation

Reported H1 FY26 (six months to 31-Dec-2025) results: record normalised EBITDAF of NZ$307m (+38% YoY), NPAT up 36% to NZ$95m, gross margin up 27% to NZ$521m; declared interim dividend of 7.30 cents per share
Rights offer settlement/allotment completed on NZX and ASX; ~192.8m new shares issued (~17.4% of pre-raise share count)
Held 2025 Investor Day, presenting the Gen35 Horizon 2 capital allocation framework and renewables pipeline detail

Reported FY25 annual results: reported EBITDAF NZ$454m (normalised NZ$470m, both up from FY24's $407m/$413m), NPAT NZ$169m (up from $131m), total FY25 dividend 14.3 cents per share (up from 14.0 cents); revenue NZ$3.7bn (up from $3.1bn)

Signed 10-year Huntly Firming Options (HFOs) with Meridian, Mercury and Contact covering 235 MW of Rankine capacity through 2035, plus a shared strategic coal fuel reserve (600kt funded across the four companies), subject to Commerce Commission review
Consolidated three retail brands (Genesis, Frank, Ecotricity) into a single unified Genesis brand to simplify the customer offer and cut costs (~200 fewer retail roles)

Opened Lauriston solar farm (63 MWp, Canterbury) — New Zealand's largest solar project to date — and progressed Edgecumbe, Foxton and Leeston solar developments; sold the ageing Hau Nui wind farm to focus on larger-scale wind prospects
Acquired the remaining 30% of Ecotricity and moved ChargeNet EV charging JV to a majority ownership position

Ongoing NZ regulatory reform: Electricity Authority/Commerce Commission Energy Competition Task Force progressing mandatory non-discrimination obligations for gentailers, targeted for the Electricity Industry Participation Code in early 2026 with first compliance reports due 1 July 2026

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Malcolm Johns and Chair Barbara Chapman describe FY25 as "a challenging year with four very different quarters" but say strategy execution now has Genesis "on track to deliver mid to upper $500m EBITDAF by FY28." Huntly is characterised as essential national energy security infrastructure and a growing earnings contributor via Huntly Firming Options rather than a pure legacy liability. Management frames the Feb-2026 equity raise as accelerating (not changing) the existing Gen35/Horizon 2 growth plan while explicitly preserving both the BBB+ credit rating and the current dividend policy — i.e., the raise funds growth capex and reduces net debt rather than substituting for dividend cuts. The H1 FY26 result was described as a "record" first half.

bull_case: High and growing dividend (14.3 cents FY25, up from 14.0 cents FY24; 7.30 cents interim FY26) with management explicitly committing to preserve the current dividend policy through the equity raise, appealing to NZ/AU income investors in a market starved of yield alternatives

Huntly's flexible/dispatchable capacity is being repositioned from a stranded-asset risk into a contracted, fee-based earnings stream via 10-year Huntly Firming Options with the other three gentailers, reducing reliance on volatile spot generation margins

Credible, funded growth pipeline (~$2bn) across solar, wind, BESS and Huntly firming, with clear FY28 EBITDAF guidance (mid-to-upper $500m, up from $470m FY25) and an accelerated timeline post the Feb-2026 capital raise

Structural tailwind from NZ's 60-95-100 electrification target and declining domestic gas supply, which increases the value of Genesis's diversified, flexible generation portfolio relative to single-technology peers
51% Crown ownership provides an implicit floor on credit quality/governance stability and could be seen as a quasi-sovereign backstop, even though it caps takeover optionality
bear_case: Dividend sustainability is a live question: FY25 payout ratio was high (reported ~92% by some estimates) against a capex-heavy, dilutive equity raise just completed, and any hydrology-driven earnings miss would pressure the payout

Regulatory risk is rising, not falling — the Electricity Authority/Commerce Commission's Energy Competition Task Force is actively designing mandatory non-discrimination rules targeted for mid-2026 that could compress gentailer wholesale/retail margins, and the Huntly Firming Options themselves still require Commerce Commission clearance

Structural decline in NZ gas supply (down ~40% in a few years) and the depleting 46%-owned Kupe field increase Genesis's reliance on more expensive coal and imported/volatile gas at Huntly, raising both cost and emissions/ETS exposure

Retail and gas market share both fell in FY25 (electricity 24.0%→22.9%, gas 35.6%→33.3%), suggesting the brand consolidation and cost-cutting have not yet stemmed competitive losses to independents and peers

Large near-term capital intensity (renewables build, BESS, hydro stay-in-business capex, technology transformation spend peaking in FY26) creates execution risk and keeps free cash flow constrained even as EBITDAF guidance points higher, with the FY28 targets explicitly conditioned on "average hydro conditions" and "no major plant outages"
